newsitem.title: USA: Only a "palace revolution" in house of labor?.
newsitem.headline: Only a "palace revolution" in house of labor?.

text.p: The AFL-CIO has undergone a "palace revolution at the top which has not percolated down to its members," an authority on democracy in the House of Labour says.

"The great untapped resource of the labour movement is its own 13 million members. And so far they haven't been inspired that it's their movement," said Herman Benson, founder and secretary-treasurer of the Association For Union Democracy, or AUD, in Brooklyn-based non-political, gadfly outfit that aids members of union locals who battle for fair hiring practices, free speech, and open elections in their union halls.

Just the fact that those backing John Sweeney mounted a successful campaign against incumbent Lane Kirkland to make him AFL-CIO president last year "legitimized the whole idea of being in opposition," Benson said, and put heart in the reformers. However, he added, in some union locals, fair and open elections are non-existent.

Since about 1,000 member of union locals turn to AUD annually for help, Benson has a pretty good idea of which union bosses block reformers from running against them, voting, or so much as airing a gripe at a meeting.
The locals AUD doesn't hear from, Benson said, "are those that are perfect, so no complaints, and those where people are so scared they don't open their mouths."

At 81, Benson likely knows trade unionism as well as anyone. Prior to founding his non-profit group in 1969, he devoted 25 years to making tools in Detroit and still proudly carries a United Auto Workers' union card.

Unions Benson cites for their democratic practices include the UAW, the United Mine Workers, the American Federation of Teachers, the Marine Engineers Beneficial Association and the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, which he said is now "one of the most democratic."

Six years ago, AUD filed a friend of the court suit which, Benson said, suggested guidelines to the federal judge who supervised the election that brought Teamsters reform candidate Ron Carey to power. Carey claimed victory last week in his re-election fight against James P. Hoffa.
There are some unions, though, Benson said, that are in need of improving their electoral procedures. Among them are:

-- The 600,000-member International Association of Machinists & Aerospace Workers, which, Benson said, may bar candidates from running for elected office if they have not attended half their local's meetings.
IAMAW Spokesman Robert Kalaski said that such a ban "is not in our constitution" but added that "we have an option that locals can write it into their bylaws and in most cases we will approve it."

-- The United Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners of America, Benson said, has been "putting locals under district councils," which deprives them "of control over their own dues" and has abolished the right to elect business agents.
The district council votes "Yes" or "No" on contracts, Benson said, "and if the (local) members don't like it, tough."

A UBCJ spokesman retorted that the councils operate "on the same principle as our government -- representative democracy" and that "leaders are elected and given the authority to do the job they are chosen for."
-- The 80,000-member Seafarer's International Union, which Benson scored for its "long history of repression of members' rights."
An SIU spokesman rejected the charge as "Absolutely ridiculous and without foundation, a fantasy of a man who makes his living irresponsibly by attacking unions."
-- The Service Employees International Union, Benson said, is "one of the best in the country." But he called its New York local "horrible."

The U.S. Court of Appeals last summer ordered the local's president, Gus Bevona, and his aides to repay their treasury $19,343 paid to investigators to shadow Carlos Guzman, Bevona's political opponent.

Guzman, a carpet cleaner at the World Trade Centre, was awarded $104,641 because he was "scared out of his life," said his lawyer, Jack Raisner, a law professor at St. John's University in New York. "They had him surveilled by what he thought was a Mafia wipe-out squad."

Guzman's Members for a Better Union seeks to allow more members to vote on bargaining pacts, to chop Bevona's salary from over $400,000 to $120,000, and to elect shop stewards, who are now picked by officers.
Bevona's press aide said stewards are "usually appointed by business agents" who "sometimes hold informal elections if there are two responsible, competent people who want to be shop stewards."
To whom did Guzman turn for help when he decided to clean SEIU's house? -- Benson, who advised him on how to proceed and who wrote up his fight in AUD's journal, "Union Democracy Review."
What the House of Labour needs, Benson believes, is more Guzmans, fewer Bevonas and democratic reforms that spread beyond the "palace" grounds.
(EDITORS: Sherwood Ross is a freelance writer who covers workplace issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Ross.)
